text: Morning. Can you hear me okay? I think my headset decided today was the day.

text: Great. So, um, Tom's dialling in a few minutes late, he's got something running over. Shall we start and catch him up?

text: Okay. So before we get into it — I actually spent three years at a freight forwarder before I moved into software. Middle office, mostly. So when your team said "we run onboarding out of a spreadsheet" I did have a bit of a flashback.

text: [laughs] Which spreadsheet?

text: Right. Okay, so my plan for today, roughly — I want to spend the first chunk just understanding how you actually handle this, and then Jon can show the parts of the product that map onto that. Not the full tour. I'd rather skip the bits that aren't relevant.

text: Please. I've sat through the full tour from three vendors this quarter.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Understood. So — where does it hurt?

text: The short version is we've got too much operational work living between systems. And I want to be clear up front, we're not looking for another dashboard. We've got dashboards. We need something that actually moves work along and makes it visible who owns what.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Can you give me a concrete one?

text: Sure. Handoffs between sales, onboarding and customer success. All of that is managed through spreadsheets and Slack reminders. So renewal risks and implementation blockers get noticed late. Not never — late.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: How late is late?

speaker: Rachel Morgan
text: Depends. Sometimes a week. Sometimes we find out at the QBR, which is — yeah.

text: And is it that the steps are manual, or —

text: That's the pattern we see most, actually. Connecting systems is one problem. Operating the process that sits on top of the connections is a different problem, and the second one is usually where the pain is.

speaker: Rachel Morgan
text: Yeah.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Do you have numbers on it, or is it anecdotal?

speaker: Rachel Morgan
text: Mix. We've got outcome metrics. The operational telemetry is weak. We can usually tell you something was late after the fact. We're much worse at answering why it was late, or which dependency failed, or whether the same thing happened fifteen times last month.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: That last one is the one that costs you.

speaker: Rachel Morgan
text: That's the one that costs us, yes.

text: — sorry, sorry, I'm here. Sorry. Was on with a customer.

text: Right. Well, my angle is slightly different from Rachel's. I want to make sure we don't buy a tool that looks great in a demo and then becomes another thing my team has to babysit. We've already got automation nobody quite owns.

text: Say more on that.

text: We have at least two scripts running that I could not tell you the author of.

text: Okay. Look, I'm going to jump ahead slightly because I'd rather you hear this early than at minute fifty-five —

speaker: Rachel Morgan

speaker: Rachel Morgan

text: So I don't want to frame this as "we have no automation." The question is whether a different layer gives us better maintainability and operational control.

text: That's a much better framing than most people give us, honestly. And to be clear, we're not trying to replace every integration platform. text: That's exactly the right level to test at, and it's the bit I'd want you to push on. Workflows are event-driven but each run holds state. speaker: Tom Alvarez
text: Can the queue be owned by a team? Not a named person. People change roles constantly here and individual ownership is genuinely one of the reasons our current stuff breaks.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Yes. Route to a group, resolve a person dynamically from a field, or use an on-call style fallback. And the run history persists, so an admin can see the inputs, which steps ran, where it stopped.

speaker: Tom Alvarez
text: Okay. That's better than what we've got.

speaker: Rachel Morgan

text: One thing I noted from your pre-call form — you've got roughly a hundred and forty customer-facing users but you'd only expect twenty-five to actually build or administer workflows?

speaker: Rachel Morgan

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Okay, that matters for the commercial model. Maya will come back to it.

text: You'd mentioned AI in your notes. I'll be brief on it because I don't think it's the centre of gravity here. Classification, summarisation, extracting fields from text, drafting something for a human to approve.

speaker: Rachel Morgan
text: Good. I'm wary of the word agent, mostly because it usually means nobody can explain why something happened.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: That's a reasonable prior.

speaker: Rachel Morgan
text: Where would you use a model versus just rules?

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Rules for anything already structured and safety-critical. Model where the input is genuinely unstructured or the task is semantic. Summarising a long ticket thread, fine. Deciding whether to issue a refund above a threshold — that should stay deterministic and permissioned.

speaker: Tom Alvarez
text: Can we see the prompt and the model config? And can we switch AI off entirely for a workspace?

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Yes to both. AI steps are explicit, inspectable steps. Admins can restrict which models are allowed. Enterprise customers can disable AI features outright. We log the model configuration used for a run. And we don't use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model.

speaker: Rachel Morgan
text: That last one needs to be in writing. Not in a demo.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Noted, and agreed — that belongs in the contract, not on a call.

speaker: Tom Alvarez
text: Can the thing refuse to answer if the source material is thin? The failure mode I dislike is a very confident summary built on one incomplete note.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: You can design for that. Require a minimum set of fields or sources before the AI step runs, ask the model to return structured confidence, route low-confidence cases to review. I wouldn't sell you model confidence as a mathematical guarantee though. The better control is usually evidence plus workflow policy.

speaker: Rachel Morgan
text: For anything customer-facing or exec-facing I'd want a link back to the underlying records. People need to be able to challenge the output.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: That's how we think about it in production too — not just "did the model answer", but did it use the right records, were the key facts preserved, did the uncertain cases get escalated.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Let me show you run history, actually, because it's related. [pause] So — filter by workflow, status, time, or a business field. Open a run, you get every step, inputs, outputs, timing, retries, any human approval.

speaker: Tom Alvarez
text: Who can see the payload? We'll have workflows where an admin should know a step failed without necessarily seeing all the customer data in it.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Permissions can separate workflow administration from business viewing. I'd flag that exact field-level masking requirements should be part of security design rather than something I promise now. We do support role-based access, workspace separation, and secrets aren't displayed in run logs.

speaker: Rachel Morgan
text: Can we get metrics out into our own monitoring? I don't want operationally critical automation only visible inside a vendor console.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Run events and metrics through APIs and webhooks, and audit export on Enterprise. Several customers forward failures into their incident tooling. Happy to show actual payloads in a technical session.

speaker: Tom Alvarez
text: That matters to me a lot more than a nice dashboard.

speaker: Rachel Morgan
text: Version history — if someone changes a condition on a Friday afternoon and it breaks, can we see exactly what changed?

text: Version history and change metadata, yes. Rollback and promotion patterns vary a bit by workflow and package. For your evaluation I'd actually suggest we include a change-management scenario rather than just building the thing once.

speaker: Tom Alvarez
text: Yes. That's closer to real life.

speaker: Rachel Morgan
text: That's a good answer.

speaker: Tom Alvarez
text: That separation would help. AI's interesting but it's not worth blocking the automation case over.

text: So when something changes I change it in one place.

speaker: Sophie Reed
text: Okay. That is the most compelling thing you've said.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: I'll take it.

speaker: Sophie Reed
text: What about visibility of who owns what? Because the dead-employee problem is real.

text: Version history and change metadata on every workflow. So you can see what changed and when. And you'd typically define who can publish to production versus who can build in a dev workspace.

speaker: Marcus Lee
text: We don't have a dev workspace. We don't have a dev anything.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: [laughs] You'd get one. That's not extra cost, it's just how it's structured.

text: Do you do the AI stuff? Everyone does the AI stuff now.

speaker: Sophie Reed
text: Is there something there for us or are you being polite?

text: There might be one. You mentioned wanting a weekly digest of recurring support reasons pushed to the e-commerce and product teams?

text: With links. Because I don't trust a summary I can't verify.

speaker: Sophie Reed
text: Does that cost extra?

text: Usage is scoped on workflow runs and premium connectors. I'd want to model that for your volumes rather than say "no" and surprise you later.

speaker: Sophie Reed
text: Everyone says that and then there's a surprise later.

text: Then let me put the assumptions in writing and you can hold me to them.

speaker: Sophie Reed

speaker: Sophie Reed
text: I can choose tools under fifteen thousand a year on my own. Above that it goes to the COO and the finance director.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: And eighteen hundred a month is —

speaker: Sophie Reed

speaker: Marcus Lee
text: And nobody here knows Make except Sophie.

speaker: Sophie Reed

speaker: Sophie Reed

speaker: Sophie Reed
text: [inaudible]

text: — sorry. Sorry. Back. My office wifi is genuinely worse than my house wifi and I don't understand why.

speaker: Sophie Reed

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Good afternoon. Martin, Anika — thank you both.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: Good afternoon.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: Hello.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: I sent an agenda but I'd rather you told me if it's wrong.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: It's mostly right. I would change one thing. You have a product demonstration in the middle. I don't want that today.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Okay. Tell me why, so I understand the shape of this.

text: Because if the deployment architecture doesn't work, the product is irrelevant. We have bought software before that demonstrated beautifully and then could not reach our systems. I would rather spend the hour on architecture and governance and see the product later, if there is a later.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: That's completely reasonable and honestly it makes my job easier. Jon, you're driving most of this then.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Happy to.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: I would also like to move governance earlier. I have to leave at fifty past and governance is my part.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Then let's do governance and architecture first, current state woven through, and commercials at the end — and if we don't reach commercials, we don't reach commercials.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: That is acceptable.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Anika, start us off. What does your governance function actually need to see?

speaker: Anika Bose
text: There is a long list and I will send it formally, but the headline items are SAML, SCIM, audit logs, IP restrictions, role separation, private connectivity options, disaster recovery documentation, penetration test material, and German or EU data residency.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: That is a comprehensive list.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: It is a normal list for us. I am not trying to be difficult.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: No, I didn't take it that way. Jon, take the ones you can answer now and be explicit about the ones you can't.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Right. SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning — both supported, both on Enterprise. Audit logs cover administrative and workflow events. Encryption in transit and at rest. Retention is configurable within supported ranges. SOC 2 Type II is our baseline. EU data residency is available on Enterprise.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: I said German or EU. Which is it?

speaker: Jon Bell
text: EU. I am not going to tell you we have a German region because we don't.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: [pause] Thank you for the direct answer. EU may be sufficient. It depends on which entity the data belongs to, and that is a question for our legal team, not for you.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: On IP restrictions and private connectivity — I want to be careful. There are controls available, and there are patterns customers use for private network access, but "private connectivity" means at least four different things depending on who says it. Can you tell me what you mean specifically?

speaker: Anika Bose
text: Martin, this is more yours.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: We have systems that will not be exposed to the public internet. Some of them by policy, some of them by physical network design. If your platform must call them over the internet, that is not possible for those systems.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Understood. So the pattern there is generally an agent or a controlled gateway sitting inside your network that the platform communicates with, rather than direct outbound calls to your systems. But I want to validate that against your actual environment rather than describe it in the abstract.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: That is the answer I expected and it is the answer I wanted.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: Disaster recovery documentation and pen test material — you have these?

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Yes, both available under the normal security process, along with SOC 2, subprocessor list, DPA, and an architecture diagram.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: Good. Send all of it. We will also send our questionnaire. It is two hundred and forty questions.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: We'll complete it.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: Everyone says that.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: We will complete it. If there are questions we can't answer we'll say "no" rather than "partially".

speaker: Anika Bose
text: That would be unusual.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: [laughs] I'll try to be unusual.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: There is one more governance item and it is not a technology item.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: The works council. The Betriebsrat. If a workflow monitors employee activity in any way — for example if it measures how long an individual takes to complete an approval — that is a co-determination matter and it must go through the works council.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: How long does that take?

speaker: Anika Bose
text: It varies. Three months is optimistic. Six is realistic if the use case is contested.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Six months.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: Six months. This is why I want it discussed now and not in October.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Can I ask a clarifying question? Is the issue that the data exists, or that it is used for individual performance assessment?

speaker: Anika Bose
text: That is the correct question and the answer is the second one, mostly. If the system records that a step took four days, that is process data. If the system reports that Herr Müller took four days, and that report goes to his manager, that is a different thing.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: That's genuinely designable. You would aggregate at the queue or team level rather than the individual level, and you would restrict who can view run-level detail. It's a permissions and reporting design question.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: If you can show me that design, it helps my case with the works council considerably.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Let's make that an explicit deliverable rather than a conversation. Jon, can you write a short note on team-level versus individual-level visibility?

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Yes. And I'd want to be clear in it about what the platform records versus what it exposes, because those are different.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: Yes. Exactly that distinction.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: Can I add something here? This is the kind of thing that kills projects at DeltaWorks. Not the technology. The technology usually works. It's that we discover in month five that a use case requires a process we didn't budget six months for.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Then let's flush those out today. Anika, is there anything else in that category?

speaker: Anika Bose
text: Regional IT will have opinions. That is not a formal gate but it is a real one. And procurement has a standard process that takes as long as it takes.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Understood.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: Should we do current state? Because I think it will make the architecture discussion concrete.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Please.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: Our cross-system business processes rely on nightly jobs and email approvals. That is the honest description. A batch runs at two in the morning, someone gets an email at eight, they approve it or they don't, and if they don't nothing happens until someone asks.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: And the failure mode?

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: Silence. The failure mode is silence. And then, because local teams are not stupid, they create unofficial scripts to work around it. Which are difficult for central IT to govern because central IT does not know they exist.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: We found one last year that had been running for four years.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Doing what?

speaker: Anika Bose
text: Copying data between two systems. Correctly, as it happens. But nobody had reviewed it, nobody owned it, and it used a service account with more permissions than it needed.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: The permissions part is Anika's nightmare. The "nobody owned it" part is mine.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Do you have telemetry on how often things stall, or is this anecdotal?

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: A mixture. We have outcome metrics — order cycle time, that sort of thing. Operational telemetry is weak. We can tell you something was late. We are much worse at telling you why, or which dependency failed, or whether the same pattern occurred fifteen times last month.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: That last question seems to be universal.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: I imagine it is.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Talk me through the stack.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: SAP S/4HANA. Salesforce. ServiceNow. Microsoft Teams. And several on-premise SQL Server systems, which are the ones that will cause you difficulty.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Which of those is the system of record?

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: It depends on the object, which I know is an unsatisfying answer. Commercial and customer data has a clear home. Tasks and tickets have another. Master data is SAP and that is not negotiable. And then a great deal of actual working context lives in Teams, which is precisely the problem.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: And you have MuleSoft today.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: We own MuleSoft, yes. And I want to be precise about this because people misunderstand it. MuleSoft is our integration backbone. It is good at that. It is not a tool that business operations should be using directly, and I would not want it to become one.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: So you're not looking to replace it.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: No. I am looking for the layer above it. The layer where a human decision happens, or an exception has to be routed, or three departments have to hand something to each other.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: That's exactly how we'd position it, and I'd rather you said it than me. We're not trying to replace an integration platform. Some customers keep an iPaaS or internal services for deep systems integration and use us for business-owned workflows.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: Then we agree on the shape.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: I would add a governance concern to that. If business operations own workflows, business operations must not own credentials.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Agreed, and that's how it's structured. Connections and credentials are centrally managed and referenced by workflows. A builder uses a connection; they don't see the secret. Rotation happens at the connection layer, so you don't edit every workflow when a credential changes.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: And secrets do not appear in logs?

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Secret values are not displayed in run logs, no.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: Good.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: Can I correct something I said, actually. Earlier — and in the pre-call form, I think — I described us as cloud-first. That is corporate policy. speaker: Maya Chen
text: That's a significant caveat.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: It is significant for you specifically, which is why I am saying it now.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Are those two plants in scope for the first use case?

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: [pause] Not necessarily. That is a good question. Possibly not.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Then I'd suggest we deliberately scope them out of phase one and treat them as a phase two architecture question. Otherwise the hardest constraint in your estate drives the design of the easiest use case.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: That is sensible. Anika, do you object?

speaker: Anika Bose
text: No. But it must be documented as deferred, not as solved.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Absolutely. Deferred, with the open question written down.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Let me try a phase-one candidate and you tell me if it's wrong. A large service contract closes in Salesforce. We validate the customer and product data against SAP. We create implementation tasks in ServiceNow. And we escalate mismatches before order processing rather than after.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: [pause] That is close. The last part is the valuable part.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Say more.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: Today the mismatch is discovered in order processing, which is downstream, which means someone in the plant is already planning against wrong data. If we caught it at contract close it would save — I don't have a number, but it is meaningful.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Could you get a number? Even roughly?

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: I could ask. I would rather give you a real one later than an invented one now.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: That's fine, and it's the right instinct. We'd want to baseline it before automating anyway.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: One caveat on the workflow. The happy path is not the difficult part.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Everyone says that and everyone's right.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: Then I will say it too. I want to see what happens when data is missing, when SAP does not respond, when an approver does nothing for two days, and when the account changes state after the workflow has already started. That last one is common with us because contracts get amended.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: That's the right level to test. Workflows are event-driven but each run holds state. So you can branch on data, pause for approvals, retry external actions, set timeout rules, and push an exception into a queue rather than failing silently.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: And if the contract is amended mid-run?

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Then you'd typically design for it explicitly — either the workflow re-reads state at decision points rather than trusting what it captured at trigger time, or you have a cancellation path that a second event can invoke. Both are patterns rather than switches. I'd want to design that one with you.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: That is an honest answer. Most vendors say "yes, it handles that."

speaker: Jon Bell
text: It handles it if you build it to. It doesn't handle it by magic.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: Can the exception queue be owned by a team rather than a named individual? Our people change roles constantly and individual ownership is one of the reasons our current automations decay.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Yes. Route to a group, resolve a person dynamically from a field, or use an on-call style fallback. Run history persists, so an administrator can see inputs, which steps ran, and where it stopped.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: And who can see the payload in that history?

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Permissions can separate workflow administration from business viewing. Field-level masking for specific payloads is a design conversation rather than a checkbox — I don't want to say "yes, masking" and have you discover the nuance later.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: I have written "design conversation" three times now.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: [laughs] I know. I'd rather that than three promises.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: I agree, actually. It is unusual.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: Let me ask the SAP question directly, because it is the one that decides this.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: How do you connect to SAP S/4HANA?

speaker: Jon Bell
text: There are a few routes and which one is right depends on your landscape. speaker: Martin Vogel
text: It is definitely not one thing.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: What I'd want, before anyone talks about a pilot, is a list of the specific SAP operations phase one needs. Not "SAP integration" — the actual reads and writes. Then I can tell you which are straightforward, which are API work, and which are genuinely hard.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: I can produce that list.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: That would change this conversation from architecture in the abstract to architecture with numbers in it.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: How long would you need with the list?

speaker: Jon Bell
text: A week, and I'd want an hour with whoever owns your SAP interfaces rather than reading a spreadsheet in isolation.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: That can be arranged.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Can I flag something commercial that's hiding in this? If phase one requires significant SAP and on-premise work, that's professional services, and I'd rather price it honestly up front than have it appear after architecture review.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: Thank you. That is exactly the thing I was going to raise later.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Then let's raise it now.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: The headline licence price is not going to surprise me. We buy enterprise software. What I care about is transparency around professional services, premium connectors, and anything we would only discover after an architecture review. That is where the surprises live.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Then here's what I'll commit to. speaker: Martin Vogel
text: If you do that, you will be the second vendor this year who has.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Who was the first?

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: [laughs] I'm not going to tell you that.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Fair enough. For the record — Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement, but that's not your shape. You're an Enterprise conversation. Custom priced, advanced governance, security capabilities, higher usage.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: Yes, obviously.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: What is a user? We may have twenty people building and several hundred who only approve something.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Builders and full workspace users are the licensed users. Approval-only or notification-only populations can be structured differently depending on package. I'm not going to give you a number today because without the user model any number is misleading.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: Please put that in the proposal explicitly. I do not want to discover in year two that every occasional approver requires a full seat.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: It'll be explicit.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: There is a second use case I should mention, not for phase one.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Go on.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: Replacing several departmental Python scripts with centrally visible automations and approvals. The four-year-old script Anika mentioned is not unique. We think there are — Anika, what was the estimate?

speaker: Anika Bose
text: We identified thirty-one. We believe there are more.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Thirty-one that you know about.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: Thirty-one that we know about. Yes.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: That's a genuinely good second-phase use case, and I'd note it's a different kind of value than the first one. The first one is cycle time. This one is risk reduction and auditability.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: For me it is the more interesting one.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: For finance it is the less interesting one, which is why it is phase two.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: [laughs] That is accurate.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: I'd argue you can put a number on it. Not savings — avoided incident cost. But that's a harder internal sell and I wouldn't lead with it.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: No. Lead with cycle time.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Environment separation — you'd flagged wanting separate developer, test and production workspaces with change control.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: That is not negotiable. We do not put anything into production that has not been through test, and we do not let the person who built something be the only person who approves it.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Workspace separation is supported and Enterprise has stronger governance around who can publish where. There's version history and change metadata on every workflow. speaker: Martin Vogel
text: Our promotion process is documented. I will send it.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Then I'll map it against what the platform does and tell you where the gaps are. There will be gaps — there always are — the question is whether they're gaps you can live with.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: I would also like the change-management scenario included in any evaluation. Not just "build the workflow." Build it, change it, break it, roll it back.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: That's a better evaluation than most customers design. Yes.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: Anika designs our evaluations.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: Somebody has to.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Can I ask about naming and standards? You mentioned governance of local scripts. What would you want in place before business teams start building?

text: Naming conventions. Change control for anything classified as important. A rule that somebody other than the creator can understand each production workflow. And a register — I want to be able to answer the question "how many automations do we have" without a discovery project.

text: That matches our recommended operating model almost exactly. A few centrally owned templates, defined publishing rights, dev separated from prod, and a small central group owning standards while business teams contribute requirements.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: Who does that in practice at your other customers? A team? A person?

speaker: Jon Bell
text: Usually a small team, two to four people, sitting in whatever function is closest to the process. Sometimes IT, more often operations. The pattern that fails is when it's one person's side project.

speaker: Martin Vogel
text: We have a lot of one-person side projects.

speaker: Jon Bell
text: I know. That's why I mention it.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: I have twelve minutes. Can we do the AI question? Because I have a position on it and I would rather state it than have it discovered.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Please.

speaker: Anika Bose
text: My position is that I do not want generative AI in the first phase at all. Not because I object in principle. speaker: Maya Chen
text: That's a strategically sound position and I'm not going to argue with it.

speaker: Anika Bose

text: Then that maintenance burden is a real cost and it should be in the business case, not discovered later.

text: I'll send exact numbers, but roughly — the step from two fifty to three fifty is the significant one. Three fifty to four hundred is a smaller increment because of how the tiers are shaped.

text: So we should take four hundred.

text: Would you do three years?

text: I looked at that one before this call. It went to second line, then to engineering, then it sat.

text: It sat for eleven days and there's no good explanation. I've raised it internally and the honest answer I got was that it fell between two teams.

text: What I can do is name a specific engineer as the escalation contact for SAP issues on your account. What I can't do is promise you a resolution SLA on connector defects, because we don't offer one and I'm not going to invent it at a renewal.

text: Then you know.

text: I'll check in December.

text: [laughs] I'm sure you will.

text: Of course.

text: Alright.

text: I wasn't counting.

text: You were, but that's fine.

text: That's fair.

text: It's also accurate.

text: Forty minutes.

text: Forty minutes and a Confluence page that was last edited in November.

text: The Confluence page is quite good, in fairness.

text: I took over your account in May. It should have been the first thing I did and it wasn't.

text: There is a training portal.

text: I know there is. I've never opened it.

text: Nobody opens it.

text: [laughs]

text: Which six?

text: [pause] It's been running since January?

text: I'd rather know.

text: The three claims triage ones concern me more than the temp one. Those were the reason you bought.

text: Which do you believe?

text: So the situation is that half of what we bought this for might move somewhere else, and the other half — broker onboarding — is stalled for a completely different reason.

text: Which is?

text: Nobody's building anything. We've got four builder licences. One person uses it. She's brilliant, she's called Ellie, and she's been on maternity leave since June.

text: So you have a bus factor of one and the bus arrived.

text: The bus arrived, yes.

text: We tried to get two people up to speed in July. It didn't take.

text: Why not?

text: They're busy. And the learning curve for the first workflow is steeper than the marketing suggests.

text: How steep?

text: One of them spent two days on it and produced something that didn't work, and then went back to their actual job. Which I entirely understand.

text: Did they ask for help?

speaker: Nadia Rahman
text: No.

text: Would they have known who to ask?

speaker: Nadia Rahman
text: [pause] Probably not.

text: That's the bit I can actually fix.

text: Can you?

text: Please.

text: Go on.

text: Enterprise gives you SAML SSO and SCIM, EU data residency, audit export, advanced workspace governance, the ability to disable AI features, priority support. Nadia, how many of those are you using?

text: SSO, obviously. Audit export — no. Residency — we're UK only and we're on the EU region, so, technically yes, but it's not a requirement anyone's written down.

text: Advanced workspace governance?

text: We have one workspace.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Right.

text: What's the alternative?

text: Growth. Eighteen hundred a month, up to thirty users, annual. You'd lose SCIM, audit export, EU residency as a contractual commitment, some of the governance controls, and priority support drops to standard.

speaker: Nadia Rahman
text: We'd lose SSO?

text: SAML SSO is Enterprise. So yes, that's the one that would actually hurt.

text: That's a problem. Our security standard requires SSO for anything holding claims data.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Then Growth isn't viable and I've just talked myself out of my own suggestion.

text: [laughs] That was quick.

text: It's better to find out now. But it does mean the question is different — it's not "which tier", it's "is Enterprise worth it for what you're getting", and right now the honest answer is probably not, because you're getting very little.

text: So what do you suggest?

text: Two options and I'll be straight about both. Option one, you don't renew. We part on good terms, you export your workflow definitions and run data, and if the Guidewire route works out you were right.

text: You're offering me that?

speaker: Leo Grant
text: I'd rather offer it than have you sign a renewal you resent and churn next year with a bad taste.

speaker: Nadia Rahman
text: What's option two?

text: Option two is a shorter renewal with a genuine re-implementation attached. Six months rather than twelve, with a defined enablement programme, and we agree measurable criteria at the start. text: Would you discount six months?

text: Six months at the annual rate pro-rata, not at a short-term premium. So no uplift, no penalty for the shorter term. That's the concession.

text: And what would the enablement look like? Because "we'll do some training" is not going to convince my finance director.

text: Which three?

text: You'd pick. But I'd want commitment from their managers that they get the time, in writing, because otherwise it's July again.

text: That's a reasonable ask.

text: Third, we fix the estate. Delete the temp workflow, redirect the alerts away from Ravi's mailbox, review the six that are failing and decide for each one whether to fix it or kill it. I'd guess three should be killed.

text: Probably four.

text: Get the claims director in a room with Nadia and have the cross-system conversation. Not with me in the room — this isn't a vendor question.

text: [pause] That's the right answer and I've been avoiding it.

text: We've both been avoiding it.

text: Because she'll win.

text: Then that's the meeting to have. And whichever way it goes, you'd know what you're buying.

text: Because our current contract does auto-renew.

text: Three weeks.

text: I'd suggest you do exactly that. Serve notice, which stops the auto-renew, and then we negotiate the six-month option separately without a clock on it. That's the cleanest thing for you.

speaker: Tobias Lund

speaker: Grace Okonkwo
text: Then that's the control point, not the workflow.

speaker: Nina Patel

speaker: Grace Okonkwo
text: [pause] Good.

text: Fifteen minutes times about four hundred incidents a month.

speaker: Grace Okonkwo
text: That's a real number.

speaker: Nina Patel
text: I'd test it on fifty historical incidents before believing my own estimate. Generate a draft for each, have an analyst score it, and see whether the time saving is real.

speaker: Nina Patel

speaker: Grace Okonkwo
text: Which model?

speaker: Nina Patel
text: You choose, within what your administrator allows. And the model configuration used is logged per run, so you can evidence which model produced which draft.

speaker: Grace Okonkwo
text: For how long?

speaker: Nina Patel
text: Within your configured retention. What's yours set to?

speaker: Tobias Lund
text: Ninety days, I think.

speaker: Grace Okonkwo

speaker: Nina Patel
text: Then I'd check which bucket run records fall into for you, because that's the sort of thing that's assumed rather than verified.

speaker: Grace Okonkwo
text: Add it to the list.

speaker: Nina Patel
text: On the list.

speaker: Grace Okonkwo
text: Training. I know the answer but I want it said on this call.

speaker: Nina Patel
text: We do not use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model. That's in your contract, not just in the documentation.

speaker: Grace Okonkwo
text: And the model provider?

speaker: Nina Patel
text: Depends on the provider and the arrangement. We use enterprise API arrangements where those exist and the providers are documented as subprocessors. I'm not going to make a blanket statement covering every provider, because it isn't true.

speaker: Grace Okonkwo
text: Which providers are on the allowed list currently?

speaker: Nina Patel
text: I'll send the current list with the subprocessor documentation rather than reciting it and getting one wrong.

speaker: Nina Patel
text: Subprocessor change notification. The notice period is contractual and it's in your agreement.

speaker: Grace Okonkwo
text: I'll look it up.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: It's thirty days for your contract. I checked before the call because I assumed you'd ask.

speaker: Grace Okonkwo
text: [pause] Thank you. That's good account management.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: It's the only reason I get invited back.

speaker: Tobias Lund
text: [laughs]

text: The analyst catches it, because they're reviewing. But the failure mode you should actually worry about is not the obvious error — it's the plausible one. A summary that says the incident was contained at 14:20 when it was 16:20. Nobody catches that by reading, because it reads fine.

speaker: Nina Patel
text: The control is not putting facts in the summary that the analyst has to verify. Times, asset counts, classifications — those should be templated from the record directly, not generated. Let the model write the prose around fixed facts.

text: Then that's a bug in your current process and you can fix it independently of any of this.

text: It'll be in the renewal papers.

text: Governance, and it's small but it's the kind of thing that isn't small in eighteen months. You've got six builders and no defined promotion process. Anyone can publish to production.

text: It's never been a problem because it's the same six people and they're all senior.

text: It's never been a problem yet. But you're a security company with no change control on production automation, and I'd rather point that out than have your own auditor point it out.

text: How have you been operating this for eighteen months without knowing that?

text: Because nothing's broken, so I've never needed to look.

text: Enterprise supports governance around who can publish where, so the mechanism is separating build permissions from publish permissions. text: Five.

text: Couldn't, or found it hard?

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Couldn't, in the sense that the effort exceeded the value by a factor I couldn't justify to my team.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Tell me about it specifically.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Our settlement provider is a mid-sized European processor. You don't have a connector for them. Nobody does, to be fair — Workato doesn't either.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: So what was the difference?

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: The difference is that we ended up writing a custom integration either way, and once you've accepted you're writing custom integrations, you start asking what the platform is actually giving you.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: And what was the answer?

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Orchestration and run history, which are genuinely good. But not enough on their own for what we were paying.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: And this is where I'd push back on Sarah slightly.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Go on.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: The connector gap was real. But it wasn't why we left. It was the thing we pointed at.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: What was the real reason?

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Nobody in operations ever built anything.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: [pause] Say more.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: The entire pitch — and this is the pitch I bought, so I'm implicating myself — was that my team would own their own workflows. That we'd stop queuing behind engineering. Two years in, every single production workflow was built by Sarah's team.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Every one.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: [crosstalk] So we paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool. And as an engineering tool it's fine but it's not worth the premium.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Why didn't your team build?

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: [pause] A few reasons and none of them are flattering.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: I'd rather have unflattering.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: The first workflow anyone builds is hard. Not conceptually hard — fiddly. You have to understand connections, you have to understand how data moves between steps, you have to understand what happens when something's null. My operations people are good at operations. They're not good at that, and expecting them to become good at it in their spare time was naive.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Did you have enablement?

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: We had a two-day onboarding at the start. Eight people attended. Six of them never touched it again.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: And after that?

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Nothing, until you arrived in January and offered some sessions.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Which you declined.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Which I declined, because by January I'd already half-concluded it wasn't going to work and I didn't want to spend my team's time on it.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: [pause] That's useful and it's painful.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: You asked.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: I did ask. What would have changed it? If I'd arrived in month three rather than month twenty?

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Honestly, I think if someone had sat with two of my people for a week in the first quarter and got them to ship something real, we'd still be a customer.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: I agree with that.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Not a training course. Sitting with them. Building the actual thing they needed.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: We do offer that.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Do you? Nobody ever offered it to me.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: [pause] It's a paid professional services engagement.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Ah.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Which is possibly the problem. If the thing that makes the product succeed is a paid add-on, and the customer doesn't know they need it until it's too late —

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Then you've designed a product that fails by default for people like me.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: That's a harsher way of putting it than I would have, but I can't argue with it.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Can I add the engineering perspective? Because it's different.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Please.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: My team quite liked it. The run history is genuinely better than what we'd have built. The exception queues are good. When something failed at three in the morning, we could see why, and that's not nothing.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: So why did you support leaving?

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Because we were maintaining custom integrations to a platform whose main selling point was that we wouldn't have to maintain custom integrations. And because the licence cost was being justified by a benefit — business-user autonomy — that wasn't materialising.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Say the other thing.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: [pause] And because two of my engineers wanted to build it in-house and I spent eighteen months arguing against them, and eventually I ran out of arguments.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: What was your last argument?

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Maintenance. It's always maintenance. And it's a good argument right up until the platform also requires maintenance, at which point you're comparing two maintenance burdens and one of them costs a hundred thousand a year.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Is that what you're paying Workato?

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Less. Not dramatically less.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: So it isn't a price decision.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: It's partly a price decision, because at the margin we could justify one and not the other. But no, it's not primarily price.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Then what tipped it to Workato specifically?

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Two things. Their connector for our core banking platform is genuinely better than yours. That one's just true.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: It is true. We know.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: And their engineering-facing story is stronger. Recipes as code, better CI story, our engineers had opinions about it and the opinions were positive.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: So you've bought an engineering tool.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: [pause] Yes. That's fair. We've bought an engineering tool and stopped pretending.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Which is the honest conclusion. My team is never going to build workflows. That was my ambition and it was wrong, and rather than keep paying for the ambition I've accepted the reality.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Can I ask — do you think that ambition was wrong in principle, or wrong for Verity?

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: [pause] For Verity. I've seen it work elsewhere. I was at a retailer before this where the operations team genuinely did build their own things.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: What was different?

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: There was a person whose job it was. Not a champion, not an enthusiast — a role, with a title, whose entire job was building and maintaining automations for the business. Half a headcount, maybe.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: We never had that.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: We never had that and I never asked for it, because I thought the product removed the need for it.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: That's — I want to write that down properly, because I think it's the most important thing you've said.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Which part?

speaker: Maya Chen
text: That the product doesn't remove the need for the role. It changes what the role has to be good at.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Yes. That's exactly it.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: We do say that, in fairness. It's in the operating model guidance.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Is it? I've never seen the operating model guidance.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: [pause] Then we don't say it, do we.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: [laughs] Not effectively.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Let me ask about the sales process, since I ran it. What did I get wrong?

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: You want honesty on this too?

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Especially on this.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: You sold to my enthusiasm rather than to my capability. I was excited, I said my team would own it, and nobody in your organisation asked "who specifically, and what else is on their plate?"

speaker: Maya Chen
text: That's a fair criticism.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: It's not that you lied. You just believed me, and you shouldn't have, because I didn't know what I was agreeing to.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: I've started asking that question, for what it's worth. Not because of you — I don't want to claim that. But it's in my discovery now. "Name the person who'll build the second workflow."

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: That's a good question. I wouldn't have had an answer.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: That's the point of it.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Can I raise the support thing? Since we're doing grievances.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Go ahead.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: The support was inconsistent. Some tickets came back in an hour with someone who clearly understood the product. Others came back in a day with a link to documentation I'd already read and cited in the ticket.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: That's a known problem and it's a triage problem rather than a capability problem.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: I assumed as much. It's not why we left. But it contributed to a general feeling that we were a small account.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Were you treated as a small account?

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: [pause] Probably accurately, yes.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: That's the answer, isn't it. You were an eighty-thousand-pound account in a book of accounts where that's below median.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: I'd worked that out.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Most customers do.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Is there anything we could have done in the last six months? Genuinely, not rhetorically.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: [pause] Probably not. By March we'd started the Workato evaluation and once that starts it has its own momentum. People invest in it, they want to be right.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: There was a moment in April.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Was there?

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: When the Workato PoC hit the same connector problem we'd hit with you. For about two weeks it looked like we'd have the same issue either way.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: What happened?

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: They put a solutions architect on it for three days and built us a working custom connector as part of the evaluation. Not billed.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: [pause] Ah.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: That's when it was over, if you want the specific moment.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Did anyone from our side know about the connector problem in April?

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: I mentioned it on a call. Not as an emergency. As a thing I was dealing with.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: I remember that call.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: You said you'd look into whether there was a template.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: And I did, and there wasn't, and I emailed you saying there wasn't.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: You did. That was an accurate and completely useless answer.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: [pause] Yes. It was.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: I'm not attacking you. You answered the question I asked. It's just that the right response wasn't answering the question.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: The right response was three days of an SE.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: The right response was three days of an SE, yes.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Would we have done that?

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: For an eighty-thousand-pound account at renewal risk? [pause] I'd have had to argue for it. I might have lost.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: That's a thing I'm going to raise internally.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: For what it's worth, I don't think you should have kept us. I think we were the wrong customer for the product, or the product was sold to us for the wrong reason.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Which of those?

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: [pause] Both, slightly.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Alright. Let me ask about the practical side. What do you need from us for the exit?

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Workflow definitions and run history exported. I've already pulled the definitions through the API and they came out fine.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Run history?

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: That's the one I want to check. We need eighteen months of run records for audit purposes. Not for Workato — for our own compliance.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Through the run events API. I'll send the pagination details because eighteen months is a lot of records and people usually hit a limit and assume it's broken.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: That would be useful.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: How long do you need access after the contract ends?

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: When does it end?

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Thirty-first of October.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: I'd want until the end of November to be safe. The export will take longer than anyone thinks.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: I can do read-only access through November at no charge. I'd rather you had a clean exit than a scramble.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: You'd do that?

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Yes, and I'd do it for two reasons. One, it's the right thing. Two, you'll be at another company in three years.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: [laughs] That's very honest.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: It's both true things at once.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: I appreciate it either way.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: And data deletion afterwards? You'll want that documented.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Yes. Our compliance team will ask for a deletion certificate.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: I'll get that arranged and I'll tell you the timeline for it rather than saying "shortly after termination."

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Thank you.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Anything else practical?

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: There are two workflows still running that we haven't migrated. They'll be done by mid-October.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: What are they?

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Merchant onboarding notifications and a daily reconciliation report.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Neither of which will break anything if they stop.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: The reconciliation one would be noticed. Not catastrophically.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: I'll flag them so nobody deactivates anything early.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Can I ask one more question and then I'll let you go?

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Go on.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: If you were advising another operations director who was about to buy a workflow platform — any workflow platform, not ours — what would you tell them?

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: [pause] Three things. First, name the person who'll build the fifth workflow, not the first. The first one gets built by whoever's enthusiastic. The fifth one gets built by whoever's job it is.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: That's better than my version of that question.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Second — do the integration assessment before you buy, not after. We spent four months discovering that our most important integration didn't exist. That's a question you can answer in a week if you insist on it during the evaluation.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: We should have insisted.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: We should have insisted and we didn't, because everyone was excited.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: And the third?

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Third — be honest about whether you're buying a business tool or an engineering tool, because they're priced differently and they succeed differently, and if you buy one and use the other you'll be unhappy for two years.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: That's the whole thing, isn't it.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: That's the whole thing.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Can I add one for the record?

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Please.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Whatever platform you buy, get the exported definition of a real workflow during the evaluation and have an engineer read it. Not the demo. A real one, with branching. Because that tells you whether you'll be able to review changes, and it takes ten minutes, and almost nobody does it.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Someone did that to us last month, actually.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Did we pass?

speaker: Maya Chen
text: [laughs] I think so. It's ongoing.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Good.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Can I ask what would bring you back? In three years, at another company or here.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: An honest answer to "who will build the fifth workflow", and a proposal that includes whatever it costs to make that person real. If someone had said to me "this is eighty thousand for the platform and twenty-five for six months of someone sitting with your team", I might have said no. But I'd have said no with my eyes open, or said yes and it would have worked.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: That's a product and pricing point, not a sales point.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: It's a bit of both.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: It's a bit of both. I'm going to take it to our product team, and I'll tell you honestly that I don't know whether anything will change.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: That's fine. I've been on the other side of that.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Right. What you'll get from us — the run events API pagination details, read-only access through November, the deletion certificate with an actual timeline, and a note flagging the two live workflows so nothing gets switched off early.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: That covers it.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: And genuinely, thank you. Most people don't take this call.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Most people don't ask properly. You asked properly.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: I'd like to send you what I write up, if that's alright. So you can tell me if I've misrepresented anything.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: Send it. I'll read it.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: I'll read it more carefully than he will.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: [laughs] That's true. Thanks both.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Thank you. And I'm sorry about February.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: You weren't there in February.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: I was there in April.

speaker: Kwame Boateng
text: [pause] Yes. Alright. Thank you, Ruth.

speaker: Maya Chen
text: Bye both.

speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
text: Bye.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Hazel, thanks for taking this. I know you've got a lot on.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: It's fine. I've got twenty minutes.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: We won't need twenty. Just so you know the format — this isn't a save call. Your notice is served, you're leaving on the eleventh of November, and I'm not going to try to reverse that.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: Good, because you wouldn't.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: I gathered. What I'd like is to understand why, properly.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: [pause] How honest do you want me to be?

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Completely.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: Alastair, are you alright with that?

speaker: Alastair McCrae
text: Yeah. Yeah, of course.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: Right. We bought something we didn't need. That's the whole answer.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Say more.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: We're two hundred and forty people. We manage residential blocks. Our automation needs are — a tenant reports a fault, it goes to the right contractor, someone chases if it's not done in five days. That's it. That's the sophistication level.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: And you were on Growth.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: We were on Growth, at eighteen hundred a month, for thirty users, when we had four people who ever logged in.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Four.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: Four. And two of those only looked at reports.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: So you were paying twenty-one and a half thousand a year for what — two builders?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: Two builders and eleven workflows, most of which are quite simple.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Did the workflows work?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: They worked perfectly. That's the frustrating part. I've got no complaint about the product at all.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Then what are you moving to?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: Zapier. Which we had before, which we should probably never have left.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: What'll that cost?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: About two thousand a year. Maybe two and a half with the tier we need.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: So a tenth.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: A tenth, yes.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Will it do everything?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: [pause] No. We'll lose the approval steps and we'll lose the run history, which I'll genuinely miss. But nineteen thousand pounds is a member of staff for four months, and when I put it that way to my managing director, the conversation was quite short.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: That's a hard argument to counter.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: It's an impossible argument to counter. And I'd like to say — I did think about it properly. I'm not being flippant. I sat down and listed what we'd lose.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: What was on the list?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: The run history. The approval forms, because our contractor sign-off uses those and Zapier can't really do it. And the fact that when something breaks, I know within an hour rather than when a tenant rings up.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Those are the three things that matter.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: They're the three things that matter and they're worth something. They're not worth nineteen thousand pounds a year to a company our size.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Alastair, do you want to come in?

speaker: Alastair McCrae
text: Yeah — Hazel, I mean, I'm sorry it's ended up here. Is there — I mean, is there a version where we look at the pricing? Because I could go and —

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: Alastair, no. I'm not doing that.

speaker: Alastair McCrae
text: No, I understand, I just —

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: If you can do it for eight thousand now, that tells me you could have done it for eight thousand two years ago, and then I'd be quite cross.

speaker: Alastair McCrae
text: [pause] That's fair.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Hazel, can I ask about the original purchase?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: You can, and Alastair may not enjoy it.

speaker: Alastair McCrae
text: It's fine. Honestly.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: When we bought this, I was told it would scale with us. That we'd start with the fault-reporting workflow and then do compliance, and then service charges, and then contractor management. And that was true — it would have. But we never did any of it.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Why not?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: Because we're two hundred and forty people and everyone's already got a job. The roadmap I agreed to in the sales process assumed a version of Oakhill that spent time on process improvement, and we've never once had that time.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Was that discussed?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: It was discussed enthusiastically.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: [pause] By whom?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: By both of us, to be fair. I was enthusiastic too. I'm not putting this all on Alastair.

speaker: Alastair McCrae
text: I did — I mean, I remember that conversation and you were quite keen on the compliance one.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: I was extremely keen on the compliance one. I've been keen on the compliance one for three years. It has never once reached the top of my list.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: So the purchase was priced against a future that didn't happen.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: Yes. That's a good way of putting it. We paid for eleven workflows' worth of value and a plan for forty.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Is there anything we could have done?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: [pause] Yes, actually. Two things.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Go on.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: Someone should have noticed after six months that we had four users on a thirty-user plan and said something. Not sold me something. Said something.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: That's a fair criticism. We look at that data.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: Do you?

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: We look at it. Whether anyone acts on it for an account your size is a different question, and the answer is usually no.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: At least you're honest.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: What's the second thing?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: There should be a smaller plan. Something for a company that needs five workflows and three users and doesn't need thirty seats. If you'd had something at five or six hundred a month I'd still be a customer and I'd probably have done the compliance one eventually.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: There isn't one.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: I know there isn't. Alastair told me at the time.

speaker: Alastair McCrae
text: I did say that.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: You did say that, in fairness. You said the entry point is Growth and that's the entry point.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Did you consider not buying?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: I did. And I decided the fault-reporting problem was bad enough to justify it, which it was. For about a year.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: What changed after a year?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: Nothing changed. That's the thing. It kept working. But the pain it solved stopped being fresh, and the invoice kept arriving, and eventually somebody looks at a renewal and asks what this is for.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: The problem being solved becomes invisible.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: The problem being solved becomes invisible. Exactly that. Nobody remembers how bad it was.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Do you think you'll regret it?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: [pause] Possibly. I think there'll be a moment in about four months when something breaks and nobody notices for two days and I'll think, well, that used to be handled.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: And then?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: And then I'll deal with it, because that's a two-day problem and not a nineteen-thousand-pound problem.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: That's a rational position.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: I've had a lot of time to think about it. I've been putting off this decision since May.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Can I ask about the last year of service? How was it?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: Fine. Genuinely fine. I think I've raised two tickets in two years and both were answered.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Did anyone from us contact you?

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: You did, in — March? An email about a new feature.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: A product announcement.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: A product announcement, yes.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: That's not contact.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: No, it isn't.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: [pause] I'm going to be direct with you. Your account was in a segment that doesn't get an assigned CSM. I'm on this call because it's a churn, not because I've been managing you.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: I'd worked that out. You've been very good today but you clearly hadn't heard of us before Tuesday.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: Monday, actually.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: [laughs] Monday.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

speaker: Hazel Wren
text: I don't mind. It's a commercial reality. But it does rather answer the question of why nobody noticed the four users.

speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
text: It does.

speaker: Alastair McCrae
text: Can I say something?

speaker: Hazel Wren

text: [pause] That's a fair read of our website.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: You're agreeing?

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Our marketing is aimed at companies with a governance function. You don't have one, so it isn't aimed at you.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: So why are you calling?

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Because our marketing being aimed at somebody else doesn't mean the product is wrong for you. But I'd want to establish that in about four minutes rather than argue with your conclusion.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: Go on then. Four minutes.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: What are you trying to do with Tray?

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: Order-to-deployment. A customer orders a robot cell, and then there's engineering config, procurement of the long-lead parts, build scheduling, factory acceptance testing, shipping, and site commissioning. Seven stages, five systems, and about four months elapsed.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: And what goes wrong?

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: Nothing goes wrong exactly. Things just take longer than they should because stage four doesn't know stage three finished until someone mentions it in a meeting.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: How much of the four months is waiting?

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: [pause] I don't know. That's part of why we're doing this.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Okay. How's the Tray evaluation going?

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: Well. Genuinely well. Their team's been good.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Then I'd say two things. First, I'm not going to tell you Tray is bad. It isn't. We lose to them and we beat them and it usually comes down to fit rather than quality.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: What's the second?

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Three weeks in, with a decision coming, I'd be the third horse in a two-horse race, and that's usually a waste of everyone's time.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: You're talking yourself out of it again.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: I'm being realistic about it. Unless there's something in your evaluation that isn't going well, in which case I'd want to know what.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: [pause] There is one thing.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Go on.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: Our ERP. It's a mid-market system, quite niche in manufacturing. Tray don't have a connector and we're looking at building against its API, which our one back-end developer estimates at three weeks.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Do you believe the estimate?

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: [laughs] No.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Nobody ever does.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: It'll be six.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: I'd want to be honest — there's a good chance we don't have a connector either. What's the system?

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: I'd rather not say on a cold call, if that's alright.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Completely fine. Then let me answer it generally. If it's a mid-market manufacturing ERP, we probably don't have a native connector, and you'd be building against the API with our generic REST action. Which is the same three weeks. Or six.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: So no advantage.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: No advantage on that specific point, no. There might be one on what happens afterwards — who maintains it, whether it's reusable across the seven stages — but that's a subtler argument and I'm not going to pretend it's decisive.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: You keep doing this.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Doing what?

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: Conceding things.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: I'd rather concede the things that are true and be believed on the things that aren't.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: [pause] Alright. What's the argument you would make?

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Honestly, only one, and it's small. You said your one back-end developer would build the ERP integration. What happens when he's busy and someone in operations wants to change which stage triggers a notification?

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: It waits.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: For how long?

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: [pause] Depends. Weeks.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Then the question for your evaluation — for either vendor — is whether the people who own the process can change the process without him. That's testable in a week and most evaluations don't test it.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: How would you test it?

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Have someone in operations, not your developer, build one real workflow. Not with the developer sitting next to them. And see what happens.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: [pause] That's a good test.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: It's the test that predicts whether you're happy in two years. Run it against Tray — I mean that, run it against Tray, you're three weeks in and it costs you nothing.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: And if they pass?

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Then buy Tray. You'll have made a good decision for a good reason.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: [laughs] You are the strangest salesperson I've spoken to this year.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: I'll take that.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: Look — I'm not going to restart the evaluation. We've got a decision date and I'm not moving it.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: I wouldn't ask you to.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: But I'll do this. Send me something short — not a deck — on how you'd approach the seven-stage thing, and specifically on the operations-can-change-it question. If we go with Tray and it doesn't work out, I'll know who to call.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: I'd rather have that than a demo you sit through politely.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: When's the decision?

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: Mid-October. Fourteenth, I think, or thereabouts.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Would it be worth a thirty-minute call before mid-October? Not a pitch. I'd walk through how I'd structure the seven stages and you can use the thinking whichever vendor you pick.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: You'd do that knowing we'll probably go with Tray?

speaker: Leo Grant
text: You're a hundred and fifty people building robots. You'll be four hundred people in three years and you'll be buying something else. I'd rather be the person who was useful.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: [pause] That's a long game.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: It's the only game in a market this small.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: Alright. Send the note. If it's good I'll do the thirty minutes.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Can I ask one thing before you go?

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: Go on.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: The four months. Have you got a number for what a month costs you?

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: A month of delay on a cell? Roughly, we recognise revenue on commissioning, so — a month is a month of revenue on a two hundred thousand pound order.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: And how many orders in flight?

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: Eleven at the moment.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: Then if instrumenting the seven stages tells you where two weeks are going, that's a much bigger number than either vendor's licence.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: [pause] That's the slide I need for my board, isn't it.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: It's the slide you need regardless of who you buy from.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: [laughs] Send the note, Leo.

speaker: Leo Grant
text: I will. Thanks Rafael.

speaker: Rafael Santos
text: Bye.
